title: Lupus Anticoagulant: Slow in the Tube, Fast in the Body
summary: See why a lupus anticoagulant lengthens clotting tests yet causes clots, work through screen–mix–confirm with dRVVT and APTT, and learn why antiphospholipid syndrome needs persistence and a clinical event.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 38 Hit 1 (core: lupus anticoagulant is prothrombotic), Hit 2 (APS needs clinical + persistent laboratory criteria), Hit 13 (screen, mix, confirm), Trap 6 (persistence) and the Figure 38 memory anchor. Checked against Qiao 2024 and Stańczewska 2025. Pending: “immediate-acting, no incubation” and the 99th-percentile LA cut-off detail.

objectives: Explain why lupus anticoagulant prolongs clotting tests yet is prothrombotic.
Apply the screen–mix–confirm sequence with dRVVT and a sensitive APTT.
State the persistence requirement and the laboratory profile used in antiphospholipid syndrome.

scenes.title: A clotting test that runs slow — in a patient who clots
scenes.altText: A young patient with a deep-vein thrombosis and a previous miscarriage. Her screening APTT is prolonged. A puzzled token: “Long clotting time — but she makes clots?” The lab name “lupus anticoagulant” appears with three question marks.

cues.text: A young woman has had a deep-vein thrombosis and a pregnancy loss. Her APTT comes back prolonged.
A long clotting time usually suggests bleeding. Yet she is forming clots.
The culprit has a misleading name: lupus anticoagulant. It slows clotting tests in the tube, but promotes clotting in the body.

props.label: Long clotting time — but she makes clots?

scenes.title: Normal: phospholipid-dependent clotting
scenes.altText: Clotting reactions assemble on a phospholipid surface. Two screening tests use deliberately low phospholipid so that antibodies interfering with it show up: the dilute Russell’s viper venom time (dRVVT), which activates factor X directly, and a sensitive APTT, which starts with contact-factor activation. Antiphospholipid antibodies target phospholipid-binding proteins such as β2-glycoprotein I and prothrombin; in the tube they compete for the scarce phospholipid and slow clotting.

cues.text: Clotting factors assemble on a phospholipid surface. In the body, that’s the surface of activated platelets and cells.
Two screening tests for lupus anticoagulant use only a little phospholipid, so interference shows up. One is the dilute Russell’s viper venom time, which activates factor ten directly.
The other is a sensitive APTT, which starts with the contact factors. Guidelines recommend using both, because they work differently.
Antiphospholipid antibodies bind phospholipid-binding proteins such as beta-two glycoprotein one and prothrombin. In the tube, they tie up the scarce phospholipid, so clotting slows.

scenes.title: What changes: the three-step test
scenes.altText: Three steps light up in order. 1 Screen: the dRVVT and/or sensitive APTT is prolonged. 2 Mix: patient plasma mixed with normal plasma stays prolonged (an inhibitor, not a deficiency). 3 Confirm: adding excess phospholipid swamps the antibodies and the clotting time shortens — phospholipid dependence proven. A side note: other inhibitors must be excluded (e.g. anticoagulant drugs, factor-specific inhibitors).

cues.text: Step one, screen. The dRVVT or the sensitive APTT is prolonged.
Step two, mix. Adding normal plasma does not fix it, so the problem is an inhibitor, not a missing factor.
Step three, confirm. Add a large excess of phospholipid. The antibodies can’t tie it all up, so the clotting time shortens. That proves the inhibitor is phospholipid-dependent.
Before calling it lupus anticoagulant, other inhibitors must be excluded — including anticoagulant drugs and factor-specific inhibitors.

props.label: Exclude other inhibitors (anticoagulant drugs, factor inhibitors)

scenes.title: In the lab: persistence and the full profile
scenes.altText: A calendar: a positive lupus anticoagulant on day 0, repeated at 12 weeks — still positive. Classification needs at least one clinical criterion (thrombosis or defined pregnancy morbidity) plus persistently positive laboratory criteria. A profile card shows the three antiphospholipid tests: lupus anticoagulant (clotting), anticardiolipin and anti-β2-glycoprotein I (immunoassays); triple positivity carries a higher thrombotic risk. A caution token: anticoagulant therapy complicates lupus anticoagulant testing.

cues.text: One positive result is a finding, not a diagnosis. Lupus anticoagulant must be shown again at least 12 weeks later to prove it is persistent.
Antiphospholipid syndrome needs both: a clinical event — thrombosis or certain pregnancy complications — and persistently positive laboratory tests.

The laboratory profile has three parts: lupus anticoagulant, tested by clotting; and anticardiolipin and anti-beta-two glycoprotein one, tested by immunoassay. Being positive on all three — triple positivity — carries the highest clotting risk.
And anticoagulant drugs interfere with lupus anticoagulant testing, so the timing and the medication list matter.

props.title: APS = clinical + laboratory
lines: ≥ 1 clinical: thrombosis or defined pregnancy morbidity

scenes.title: Two classic traps
scenes.altText: Trap card: “Prolonged APTT from lupus anticoagulant = bleeding risk” is crossed out → “Lupus anticoagulant is prothrombotic.” Trap card: “One positive LA = antiphospholipid syndrome” is crossed out → “Needs persistence (≥ 12 weeks apart) plus a clinical criterion.”

cues.text: Trap one: a prolonged APTT from lupus anticoagulant does not mean bleeding risk. Lupus anticoagulant is associated with thrombosis.
Trap two: one positive test is not antiphospholipid syndrome. Positivity must persist on testing at least 12 weeks apart, and there must be a clinical event.
And remember the confirm step: excess phospholipid shortens the clotting time. That’s what separates lupus anticoagulant from other inhibitors.

props.label: Confirm step: excess phospholipid shortens the time

scenes.title: Slow in the tube, fast in the body
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Slow in the tube, fast in the body.” Then three stamps for the test: Screen, Mix, Confirm (“stays long, then shortens with phospholipid”). A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: slow in the tube, fast in the body. And the test is screen, mix, confirm — stays long when mixed, shortens with extra phospholipid.

Where it breaks: some samples with lupus anticoagulant do correct partly on mixing, anticoagulant drugs can mimic or hide it, cut-offs are set locally, and classification criteria have changed over time. Follow current guidance.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Three tokens: “Lupus anticoagulant: slows tests, promotes clots”, “Screen (dRVVT + APTT) → mix (stays long) → confirm (phospholipid)”, “Persistent ≥ 12 weeks + clinical event = APS”.

cues.text: Lupus anticoagulant prolongs phospholipid-dependent tests but promotes thrombosis, and it is confirmed by screening, mixing and phospholipid correction, then repeated at least 12 weeks later.

props.label: Lupus anticoagulant: slows tests, promotes clots

explanation.what: Plain language: lupus anticoagulant is an antibody that makes clotting tests run slow in the lab but raises the risk of clots in the body. Scientific terms: antiphospholipid antibodies target phospholipid-binding proteins (β2-glycoprotein I, prothrombin) and prolong phospholipid-dependent clotting tests; lupus anticoagulant is detected with two screening tests of different principle — dRVVT (factor X activation) and a sensitive APTT (contact activation).
explanation.why: In low-phospholipid reagents the antibodies compete for phospholipid, prolonging clotting; in vivo they damage endothelium, activate platelets and promote thrombosis. A mixing study shows an inhibitor (no correction), and excess phospholipid overwhelms the antibodies and shortens the clotting time.
explanation.measure: Three steps: screen (prolonged dRVVT/APTT), mix (no correction), confirm (phospholipid correction), and exclude other inhibitors. Persistence: repeat ≥ 12 weeks later. APS needs ≥ 1 clinical criterion (thrombosis or defined pregnancy morbidity) and ≥ 1 persistently positive laboratory criterion (LA, anticardiolipin, anti-β2GPI); triple positivity carries the highest thrombotic risk. Anticoagulant therapy complicates testing.
explanation.differs: Lupus anticoagulant (phospholipid-dependent inhibitor, thrombosis) vs factor-specific inhibitor (bleeding); clot-based LA testing vs immunoassays for anticardiolipin and anti-β2GPI; a single positive result vs persistent positivity.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the paradox (prolonged test, thrombosis), the three-step confirmation, the dRVVT, the 12-week repeat, and the clinical + laboratory requirement for APS.

comparisons.distinguisher: Phospholipid correction and the clinical picture.

comparisons.distinguisher: Functional clotting effect vs antibody detection.

mnemonic.text: Slow in the tube, fast in the body — screen, mix, confirm.
mnemonic.explanation: Lupus anticoagulant prolongs clotting tests (slow in the tube) but causes thrombosis (fast in the body); it is proven by a prolonged screen, no correction on mixing and correction with excess phospholipid.
mnemonic.limitation: Some LA samples partly correct on mixing; anticoagulant drugs can mimic or mask LA; cut-offs are local; classification criteria have changed (2006 revised Sapporo, 2023 ACR/EULAR).

questions.stem: A dRVVT screen is prolonged, stays prolonged after 1:1 mixing with normal plasma, and shortens markedly when excess phospholipid is added. What does this indicate?

options.rationale: Correct. Prolonged screen, no mixing correction and phospholipid correction together indicate a phospholipid-dependent inhibitor.
Incorrect. A deficiency would correct on mixing.
Incorrect. A factor VIII inhibitor is not corrected by excess phospholipid, and the dRVVT bypasses factor VIII.

questions.stem: A patient with a first unprovoked thrombosis has a positive lupus anticoagulant once. What is needed before antiphospholipid syndrome can be classified?

options.text: Repeat testing showing persistent positivity at least 12 weeks later
options.rationale: Correct. Persistence must be demonstrated; one positive is a finding, not a diagnosis.

options.text: Nothing — one positive LA with thrombosis is enough

options.rationale: Incorrect. Factor VIII does not classify APS.

options.text: A repeat test the next day
options.rationale: Incorrect. The interval must be at least 12 weeks.

questions.stem: Why is lupus anticoagulant considered prothrombotic despite prolonging clotting tests?

options.text: The antibodies slow phospholipid-dependent reactions in the tube but promote thrombosis in the body
options.rationale: Correct. In vitro they compete for phospholipid; in vivo they activate endothelium and platelets.
Incorrect. They do not consume factors; that would cause bleeding.

options.text: They are always found in systemic lupus erythematosus
options.rationale: Incorrect. The name is misleading; the antibodies occur outside lupus too.
Incorrect. That is not the mechanism.

references.usedFor: aPL target phospholipid-binding proteins, damage endothelium and activate coagulation (pro-thrombotic); dRVVT (factor X activation) and sensitive aPTT (contact activation) are the two recommended LAC screening tests; LA criteria: prolongation of ≥ 1 phospholipid-based test, failure to correct with mixing, correction with added phospholipid, exclusion of other inhibitors; APS requires ≥ 1 clinical and ≥ 1 laboratory criterion; persistence extended from 6 to 12 weeks in 2006; 2023 ACR/EULAR criteria; anticoagulation complicates testing; triple positivity.

references.citation: Stańczewska A, Szewczyk-Golec K, Hołyńska-Iwan I, et al. Antiphospholipid syndrome—diagnostic and methodologic approach. Metabolites. 2025;15(8):500.
references.usedFor: Two screening tests (low-phospholipid APTT and dRVVT); three-step procedure (screen, mixing test, confirmation); repeat after at least 12 weeks to confirm persistence; antibodies against β2GPI, prothrombin and others; triple positivity carries higher risk of venous and arterial thrombosis.

claims.text: aPL target phospholipid-binding proteins (β2GPI, prothrombin) and are prothrombotic in vivo while prolonging phospholipid-dependent tests.
Two screening tests: dRVVT (factor X) and sensitive APTT (contact).
Screen → mix (no correction) → confirm (phospholipid correction) → exclude other inhibitors.
APS: ≥ 1 clinical + ≥ 1 laboratory criterion; persistence ≥ 12 weeks; triple positivity highest risk; anticoagulants complicate testing.
LA is immediate-acting (no incubation needed), unlike FVIII inhibitors; LA is the strongest laboratory risk factor for thrombosis; positivity cut-off at the 99th percentile of ≥ 40 donors.
